name: Merge Sort
statement: Sort by splitting the list in half, sorting each half, and merging the two sorted halves.
statementAccent: splitting the list in half, sorting each half, and merging
meaning: Merge sort is an efficient, general-purpose, comparison-based sorting algorithm that uses the divide-and-conquer strategy. It works by recursively dividing the unsorted list into two halves until each sublist contains a single element, which is trivially sorted, and then repeatedly merging the sublists back together in sorted order to produce new sorted sublists, until there is a single sorted list. The key operation is the merge of two already-sorted lists into one sorted list, done in linear time by repeatedly taking the smaller of the two lists' front elements. Merge sort has order n log n time complexity in all cases, worst, average, and best, which is an advantage over quicksort's order n squared worst case. It is a stable sort, meaning it preserves the relative order of elements that compare equal, a property that matters when sorting records by one field while keeping another field's order. Its standard array version is not in-place: it typically requires order n additional memory to hold the merged output, which is a disadvantage compared with in-place sorts like quicksort and heapsort. The algorithm is generally attributed to John von Neumann, who described it in 1945. Merge sort is used where stability and guaranteed order n log n behaviour matter, and it is especially well suited to sorting linked lists and to external sorting of data too large to fit in memory, because it accesses data sequentially; it is also the basis of hybrid algorithms such as Timsort, used in Python and Java.
mechanism: Merge sort sorts by the divide-and-conquer principle, breaking the problem into halves, solving each, and combining the solutions. The divide step is trivial: the list is split into two halves, then each half is split again, recursively, until every sublist has just one element, which is by definition already sorted. The real work is in the combine step, the merge, which takes two lists that are each already sorted and interleaves them into a single sorted list. The merge is efficient because both inputs are sorted: one keeps a pointer at the front of each, repeatedly compares the two front elements, and appends the smaller to the output, advancing that list's pointer, until one list is exhausted and the remainder of the other is appended. Merging two lists of total length k takes order k time. Because the recursion halves the list about log n times, and each level of the recursion performs merges totalling order n work, the whole sort costs order n log n, and this holds regardless of the input, so merge sort has no bad case, its worst, average, and best times all order n log n, unlike quicksort which can degrade to order n squared. The merge preserves stability, since when two elements compare equal the one from the earlier list is taken first, keeping equal elements in their original relative order. The cost of this guaranteed performance and stability is space: the standard array implementation needs an auxiliary array of order n to hold merged results, whereas quicksort and heapsort sort in place. Merge sort's sequential access pattern makes it a natural fit for linked lists, which it can sort with only pointer rearrangement, and for external sorting, where data on disk or tape is read and written in long sequential runs that are merged.

examples.text: The list is halved recursively until each sublist has one element, which is already sorted.
Two sorted lists are merged by repeatedly taking the smaller front element, in time linear in their total length.
Merge sort runs in order n log n in the worst, average, and best cases, unlike quicksort's order n squared worst case.

variants.name: Timsort
variants.text: A hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort, used as the default sort in Python and Java.

whyItMatters: Merge sort is one of the fundamental sorting algorithms, valued for guarantees that quicksort cannot make and for a structure that suits data far larger than memory. Its order n log n running time holds in every case, with no bad inputs, so it offers dependable performance where a worst-case blowup would be unacceptable, and it is a stable sort, preserving the relative order of equal elements, which is essential when sorting records by one key while respecting an existing order on another. These properties make merge sort, and hybrids built on it, the method of choice in many standard libraries: Timsort, a refined blend of merge sort and insertion sort, is the default sorting algorithm for objects in both Python and Java. Merge sort is also uniquely suited to settings that quicksort and heapsort handle poorly. Because it accesses data sequentially rather than by random jumps, it sorts linked lists efficiently with mere pointer manipulation, and it is the classic algorithm for external sorting, arranging datasets too big for main memory by merging long sorted runs streamed from disk or tape, a task central to databases and big-data processing. As a teaching example it is a clean, canonical illustration of divide and conquer and of recurrence-based analysis. Generally credited to John von Neumann in 1945, it is among the oldest algorithms still in everyday use. As the method that sorts by splitting, sorting the halves, and merging them, merge sort is a cornerstone of sorting.

working.text: split the list into two halves, recursively, until each sublist holds a single element.
combine two sorted sublists into one by repeatedly taking the smaller front element.
merge the growing sorted sublists until a single sorted list remains.

limits: Merge sort is dependable but has trade-offs that reward care. Its main drawback is space: the standard array implementation is not in-place, needing order n auxiliary memory to hold merged output, which makes it costlier in memory than quicksort or heapsort, a real concern for large in-memory arrays; in-place merge variants exist but are complex and often slower. Although its order n log n worst case beats quicksort's order n squared, merge sort is frequently slower than a well-implemented quicksort in practice on in-memory arrays, because of its extra data movement and poorer cache behaviour, so the guaranteed bound comes at a constant-factor cost. Merge sort's advantages, stability and sequential access, are what distinguish it, and it shines specifically for linked lists and external sorting rather than as a universal replacement for other sorts. Some details reward care: the guaranteed order n log n and stability are the standard array version's properties, the algorithm is generally attributed to John von Neumann in 1945, and Timsort is a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort, not plain merge sort. So merge sort robustly sorts in guaranteed order n log n time, understood as a stable but not in-place algorithm best suited to linked lists and external sorting.
misreadings: Merge sort is not in-place; its standard version needs order n extra memory, unlike quicksort or heapsort. Its guaranteed order n log n does not make it always fastest, since quicksort often wins in practice on arrays. And its strengths are stability and sequential access, so treating merge sort as memory-free, as universally fastest, or as interchangeable with in-place sorts, misreads it.
origin: The stable divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm generally attributed to John von Neumann in 1945, which sorts by splitting a list, sorting each half, and merging the sorted halves in guaranteed order n log n time.
